vignette:
The Smell That Won't Leave

Fatima is a fifty-one-year-old woman who has managed a mid-sized hotel in her adopted city for nearly a decade. She is known among her staff as someone who notices everything - a smudge on a lobby mirror, a guest's hesitation at check-in, the faint smell of something burning in a kitchen that shouldn't be burning. That last instinct, the one she was always proud of, is now the thing that undoes her.

Three years ago, a maintenance contractor working in the hotel's mechanical room improperly handled a refrigerant system, releasing a cloud of ammonia-based coolant into the lower ventilation corridor. Fatima was the first manager on scene. She remembers walking toward the smell before she understood what it was - her professional reflex, always move toward the problem. Within seconds her eyes were streaming, her throat closing, and she was on her knees in the corridor before anyone reached her. She was hospitalized for two days with chemical burns to her airways. Two kitchen workers were also treated and recovered. Fatima was told she was lucky. She believes this, and she also cannot stop living in that corridor.

In the months following, she returned to work as soon as her pulmonologist cleared her. She told her husband, Tariq, that staying home would make things worse. She was right that she needed structure, but the hotel had become a landscape of triggers she hadn't anticipated. The scent of cleaning products - bleach, ammonia-based glass cleaner, even certain air fresheners used in the guest bathrooms - sends a signal through her body that bypasses thought entirely. Her chest tightens, her vision narrows, and for a few terrible seconds she is back on the corridor floor, certain she is dying. She has quietly rerouted which cleaning products the housekeeping staff use, telling them only that she prefers the alternatives.

At home, Fatima sleeps poorly. She wakes between two and four in the morning with a racing heart and a vague, suffocating dread she cannot always attach to a specific image. Some nights the dreams are explicit - she is in the corridor, or somewhere like it, and no one comes. Other nights she simply wakes already afraid. She has begun sleeping with the bedroom window cracked regardless of season, needing to know that outside air can reach her.

During the day she is functional, even impressive. Her staff would not know. But she monitors the hotel's ventilation reports with an attention that has tipped into something compulsive, and she finds herself holding her breath when she enters any enclosed mechanical space, which, in a building this size, happens often. She has started taking the long way between floors to avoid a particular service corridor that smells faintly of the original cleaning compound, even though she knows intellectually the chemical is gone.

What troubles Fatima most is what she describes as a kind of emotional flatness that has settled over her life outside of work. She and Tariq used to cook elaborate meals together on weekends - she grew up in a household where food was love, and the kitchen was always the center. Now certain spices, heated in oil, produce a sharpness in the air that makes her step back from the stove. She has not told Tariq why she has stopped cooking. She has not told him much. She describes feeling, at times, as though there is a pane of glass between herself and the people she loves, and she cannot find the door.

She came to therapy at Tariq's gentle insistence, after he noticed she had begun checking the smoke detectors in their home every night before bed. She sat in the first session with her hands folded neatly in her lap and said she wasn't sure what she expected to get out of this, that she was a practical woman, that she had survived harder things growing up. Then she paused and said, quietly, that she cannot remember the last time she took a full breath without thinking about it.
